rv.q: It's not often that a musical comes along that is as ambitious as it is emotional — and then succeeds on both counts. But 'Billy Elliot,' which opened Thursday at Broadway's Imperial Theatre, is an exceptional work that exemplifies what the best musicals are all about: collaboration.
Broadway's long, dark, dry spell of musicals is officially over.
That “Billy Elliot” is as much an elegy as a celebration is what makes it such a winner.
Broadway finally has in its over-hyped midst a major opening of road-show quality.
If "High School Musical" didn't have the Disney brand plastered all over it, I doubt that very many people would bother to go see it, even in a production as pleasing as this one.
Billy Elliot the Musical is irresistible perfection.
Billy Elliot really does have something for everyone, and that something is, gloriously, art.

Hall's script is vivid and smart and gets excellent support from the songs. He wrote lyrics, Elton John, the music. No single tune is bound to be a pop recording hit. Still, the fine score covers an array of styles - folk tunes, anthems, novelty numbers - and emotions that beautifully move the story along.
On the evidence so far, these young show-stoppers are nailing it.
Those ideals — tolerance, empathy, individual expression — are noble ones, and director Stephen Daldry and his company infuse them with irresistible heart.
The show's a mess, but it's a likable, good-hearted, overstuffed mess; you're more likely to go away feeling puzzled than feeling cheated by its unevenness.
The production is invigorating and inspiring, and the cast is multi-talented.
The sequences where Billy learns to dance under the tutelage of Mrs. Wilkinson and her accompanist Mr. Braithwaite are gorgeous.
